stem: A single card is drawn at random from a standard deck of 52 playing cards. What is the probability that the card is either a heart or a king?

per_option_rationale.rationale: P(heart or king) = P(heart) + P(king) - P(heart and king) = 13/52 + 4/52 - 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.
Student computed P(not heart and not king) = 36/52 = 9/13, the complement of the required event.
Student treated 'or' as 'and' and computed P(heart) x P(king) = (13/52)x(4/52) = 52/2704 = 1/52.
Student added P(heart) and P(king) without subtracting the overlap: 13/52 + 4/52 = 17/52.

explanation: Use the addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). There are 13 hearts, 4 kings, and exactly 1 card that is both (the king of hearts). Favorable outcomes = 13 + 4 - 1 = 16. P = 16/52 = 4/13.

explanation_sections.punchline: Hearts and kings share exactly one card. The addition rule subtracts that overlap once: (13 + 4 - 1)/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify whether A and B can occur together before writing any formula. Hearts and kings can: the king of hearts is in both groups. So use the general addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Count each set from the deck (13 hearts, 4 kings, 1 card is both), subtract once for the overlap, then divide by 52. If the two sets were mutually exclusive, you would skip the subtraction. Confirming overlap is the first decision.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always check for an intersection before applying the addition rule. Forgetting to subtract P(A and B) double-counts every card that belongs to both groups, landing you on 17/52.
explanation_sections.timing: About 60 seconds. Identifying the overlap (king of hearts) takes 10 seconds. Three additions and one division take under 20 seconds. Distractor 17/52 is the no-subtraction trap; seeing it as a choice confirms you must check for overlap.
